The Weak Mixing Angle at Low Energies

Jens Erler 1 and Michael J. Ramsey-Musolf 2

1Instituto de Física, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 01000 México D.F., México

2Kellogg Radiation Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA

Abstract

We determine the weak mixing angle in the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme, sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu), at energy scales μ\mu relevant for present and future low energy electroweak measurements. We relate the renormalization group evolution of sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) to the corresponding evolution of α^​(μ){\hat{\alpha}}(\mu) and include higher-order terms in αs\alpha_{s} and α\alpha that had not been treated in previous analyses. We also up-date the analysis of non-perturbative, hadronic contributions and argue that the associated uncertainty is small compared to anticipated experimental errors. The resulting value of the low-energy MS¯\overline{\rm MS} weak mixing angle is sin2⁡θ^W​(0)=0.23867±0.00016\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=0.23867\pm 0.00016.

1 Introduction

The weak mixing angle is one of the fundamental parameters of the electroweak Standard Model (SM). It can be defined through the relation,

sin2⁡θW=g′2g2+g′2,\sin^{2}\theta_{W}={{g^{\prime}}^{2}\over g^{2}+{g^{\prime}}^{2}}, (1)

where gg and g′g^{\prime} are the S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} and U​(1)YU(1)_{Y} gauge couplings, respectively. Its value is not predicted and needs to be extracted from parity violating neutral current experiments, where by far the most precise results were obtained at the ZZ factories LEP 1 and SLC. Electroweak symmetry breaking provides masses for the WW and ZZ bosons proportional to their gauge interactions. Therefore, one has the additional relation,

sin2⁡θW=1−MW2MZ2,\sin^{2}\theta_{W}=1-{M_{W}^{2}\over M_{Z}^{2}}, (2)

and the gauge boson mass ratio provides independent precise information on sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W}. Extracting the fine structure constant,

α=e24​π=g2​sin2⁡θW4​π,\alpha={e^{2}\over 4\pi}={g^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{W}\over 4\pi}, (3)

from the quantum Hall effect or the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, then fixes both gauge couplings. Eqs. (1) and (3) are valid at the tree level and modified by radiative corrections. As a result, the precise numerical value of sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W} depends on the renormalization scheme and scale chosen. For example, the on-shell renormalization scheme promotes Eq. (2) to a definition of sin2⁡θW≡sin2⁡θWon−shell\sin^{2}\theta_{W}\equiv\sin^{2}\theta_{W}^{\rm\;on-shell} to all orders in perturbation theory. This definition has the advantage of being directly related to a physical observable — but only to one-loop order. Since the gauge bosons are unstable particles their masses become ambiguous starting at two-loop precision.

As an alternative, one can define flavor-dependent “effective” mixing angles appearing in the ZZ vector coupling11 1 We normalize vfv_{f} without an additional factor inversely proportional to sinθWcosθW\sin\theta_{W}\cos\theta_{W}. The scale in this factor needs to be chosen of electroweak size, μ=MZ\mu=M_{Z}, even for low energy processes. This is automatically achieved by normalizing neutral-current amplitudes using ρ​GF\rho\;G_{F}, where GFG_{F} is the Fermi constant and ρ\rho the low energy neutral-current ρ\rho parameter [1] (which is free of fermionic mass singularities). Thus, this factor does not affect our discussion.,

vf=Tf−2​Qf​sin2⁡θfeff,v_{f}=T_{f}-2Q_{f}\sin^{2}\theta_{f}^{\rm\;eff}, (4)

where QfQ_{f} and TfT_{f} are the fermion charge and third component of isospin, respectively. Gauge boson self-energy and Z​f​f¯Zf{\bar{f}}-vertex corrections are absorbed into scheme dependent form factors, ρf\rho_{f} and κf\kappa_{f} that are equal to unity at tree-level. The ρf\rho_{f} are corrections to the overall coupling strengths and the κf\kappa_{f} are defined by,

sin2⁡θfeff≡κf​sin2⁡θWon−shell≡κ^f​sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ),\sin^{2}\theta_{f}^{\rm\;eff}\equiv\kappa_{f}\sin^{2}\theta_{W}^{\rm\;on-shell}\equiv\hat{\kappa}_{f}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}), (5)

where the caret marks quantities in the modified minimal subtraction (MS¯\overline{\rm MS}) scheme [?–?]. This effective sin2⁡θfeff\sin^{2}\theta_{f}^{\rm\;eff} is a useful definition as long as electroweak box contributions can be neglected; since these do not resonate this condition is clearly satisfied at LEP 1 and SLC. However, with the greater precision that could be achieved with the GigaZ option of TESLA, such boxes could become non-negligible. Thus, it is not easy to construct a definition that can be equated to a physical observable to all orders. Neither is this of practical relevance: as long as it is well-defined, sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W} can be looked upon as a mere bookkeeping device and means to compare various experimental results.

What is of practical importance, however, is the numerical value of the mixing angle used in computing a given observable in a specified renormalization scheme. Generally speaking, one expects a one-loop radiatively corrected result to be valid up to small corrections of 𝒪⁡(α2π2​sin4⁡θW)∼10−4{\cal O}({\alpha^{2}\over\pi^{2}\sin^{4}\theta_{W}})\sim 10^{-4}. On the other hand, for leptons we have,

(κℓ−1)2≈1.5×10−3,(\kappa_{\ell}-1)^{2}\approx 1.5\times 10^{-3}, (6)

which is not much smaller than a typical one-loop contribution. The reason is that κℓ\kappa_{\ell} contains top-quark mass enhancements factors, mt2/MW2m_{t}^{2}/M_{W}^{2}, that spoil the expected behavior of the perturbation series. Fortunately, such enhancement factors can be avoided by a judicious choice of definition of the weak mixing angle (or renormalization scheme), rendering the truncation error small. The MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-definition considered in this article has this property, except that small ln⁡mt2/MW2\ln m_{t}^{2}/M_{W}^{2} corrections cannot be decoupled simultaneously from all observables [5, 6].

For processes off the ZZ-pole, enhancement factors of similar magnitude as those entering Eq. (6) can arise from large logarithms ln⁡MZ2/mf2\ln M_{Z}^{2}/m_{f}^{2}, where mfm_{f} is some fermion mass. These can occur even within a specifically chosen renormalization scheme. Typically, such logarithms are artifacts of using a value for sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W} obtained at the ZZ scale (where as noted above, it is measured very precisely) in theoretical expressions for very low (or high) energy observables. In some renormalization schemes, the weak mixing angle depends explicitly on a renormalization scale parameter, which could be the t’Hooft scale, μ\mu, appearing in dimensional regularization, or the momentum transfer q2q^{2}. For others there is no explicit scale parameter, and the scale dependence is of indirect nature. In either case, the aforementioned logarithms are a potential hazard and should be avoided or re-summed if possible.

The main goal of this paper is to present an analysis of the weak mixing angle in the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme, sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), relevant for observables measured at (almost) vanishing momentum transfer. These observables include the nuclear weak charge obtained in the well-known cesium atomic parity violation measurement performed by the Boulder group [7]; the parity violating Møller asymmetry at SLAC [8]; and the up-coming measurement of the weak charge of the proton at Jefferson Lab [9]. Precision measurements of the parity violating deep inelastic e​DeD asymmetry have also been discussed as future possibilities for Jefferson Lab, as has a more precise measurement of the Møller asymmetry. The value of sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0) is particularly relevant for the interpretation of the parity violation experiments, since the vector coupling of the ZZ n Eq. (4) to electrons and protons is proportional to 1−4​sin2⁡θW​(q2)feff∼0.11-4\sin^{2}\theta_{W}(q^{2})^{\rm eff}_{f}\sim 0.1 and is, therefore, highly sensitive to the value of the effective weak mixing angle. Indeed, as noted in Refs. [10, 11], one-loop contributions to sin2⁡θW​(0)feff\sin^{2}\theta_{W}(0)^{\rm eff}_{f} reduce the magnitude of the Møller asymmetry by roughly 40% from its tree-level value, an effect generated by the large logarithms discussed above. Moreover, the presence of these large logarithms in sin2⁡θW​(0)feff\sin^{2}\theta_{W}(0)^{\rm eff}_{f} is universal to all low energy neutral current observables, though their net effect may be masked by other enhanced radiative corrections22 2 For example, the left-right asymmetry for parity-violating elastic e​pep scattering also contains large logarithms associated with the fermion anapole moment as well as non-logarithmic but large W​WWW box graphs [12, 13, 14].. Consequently, one would like to sum these universally enhanced contributions to all orders. Here, we do so using the renormalization group evolution for sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) in the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme.

The MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-definition of the weak mixing angle is, of course, not unique, and one may choose an alternate scheme in which to compute radiative corrections to electroweak observables. Nevertheless, the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme offers several advantages that motivate our adoption of it here. In particular, the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-definition of sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) follows closely the coupling-based definition in Eq. (1) with a well-defined subtraction of singular terms arising in dimensional regularization, giving rise to expressions with a logarithmic μ\mu-dependence. This dependence is governed by a renormalization group equation (RGE), and choosing μ\mu equal to the momentum transfer of the process under consideration will in general avoid spurious logarithms33 3 The presence of some logarithmically-enhanced radiative corrections, such as the anapole moment effects, cannot be cannot be eliminated by the RGE for sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu).. As we discuss below, the evolution of sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) can be related in a straightforward way to that of α^​(μ){\hat{\alpha}}(\mu), the QED coupling in the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme that has been thoroughly studied elsewhere. Doing so allows us to draw upon known results for the QED β\beta-function and – in conjunction with suitable matching conditions – to improve the precision of the Standard Model predictions for low-energy observables by incorporating various higher order effects. Indeed, although the one-loop RGE for sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) has been well-studied by others, one emphasis of the present work is the inclusion of higher order QED and perturbative QCD contributions in a systematic way. We discuss the RGE in Sections 2 and 3, and matching conditions in Section 4.

A major complication arises when the contribution of the light quark flavors is considered for μ\mu of order a hadronic scale, Λ\Lambda, or smaller. In this regime, QCD corrections to the RGE (β\beta-function) cannot be obtained using perturbative methods. An analogous problem is well-known to arise for α^​(μ)\hat{\alpha}(\mu) when its value is desired at scales similar to or greater than Λ\Lambda. We address this problem in Sections 5 and 6, as well as two appendices. We argue that the corresponding theoretical uncertainty is well below the anticipated experimental errors and provide a new estimate of this uncertainty that is substantially smaller in magnitude than the previously-quoted one [15]. Non-logarithmic contributions and some more formal aspects are discussed in Section 7 while numerical results and a plot of sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) for μ=|q2|\mu=\sqrt{|q^{2}|} – along with conclusions – are presented in Section 8. We note there our results may also be applied to the recent studies of deep-inelastic neutrino-nucleus scattering carried out by the NuTeV Collaboration [16].

2 Leading order RGE analysis

The quantity sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0) is related to s^Z2≡sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}\equiv\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) by,

sin2⁡θ^W​(0)≡κ^​(0)​sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)≡[1+Δ​κ^​(0)]​s^Z2,\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)\equiv\hat{\kappa}(0)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z})\equiv[1+\Delta\hat{\kappa}(0)]\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}, (7)

where Δ​κ^​(0)\Delta\hat{\kappa}(0) is a universal (flavor-independent) radiative correction. In this Section we are interested in logarithmic contributions to κ^​(0)\hat{\kappa}(0) of the form,

α^π​sin2⁡θ^W​ln⁡MZ2mi2,{\hat{\alpha}\over\pi\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}}\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over m_{i}^{2}},

and in particular in the scale that should be used in α^\hat{\alpha} and sin2⁡θ^W\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}, appropriate for re-summing the leading, large logarithms to all orders. These logarithms arise from scale dependent self-energy mixing diagrams where one external leg is a photon and the other one is a ZZ-boson. Thus, vfv_{f} acquires a compensating scale dependence,

v^f​(μ2+Δ​μ2)=v^f​(μ)+α^​(μ)24​π​Qf​∑i[Nic​γi​vi​(μ)​Qi]​ln⁡μ2+Δ​μ2μ2,\hat{v}_{f}\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}+\Delta\mu^{2}}\right)=\hat{v}_{f}(\mu)+{\hat{\alpha}(\mu)\over 24\pi}Q_{f}\sum\limits_{i}[N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}v_{i}(\mu)Q_{i}]\ln{\mu^{2}+\Delta\mu^{2}\over\mu^{2}}, (8)

where Nqc=NC=3N^{c}_{q}=N_{C}=3 (for quarks) and Nℓc=1N^{c}_{\ell}=1 (for leptons) is the color factor. We have written the sum in general form to also allow chiral fermions and bosonic degrees of freedom (to put the W±W^{\pm} and Higgs ghosts on the same footing as the fermions and to facilitate the discussion in Section 7), where the spin dependent factors γi\gamma_{i} are shown in Table 1.

With these conventions, the factor of 1/24 also appears in the lowest order QED β\beta-function coefficient,

μ2​d​α^d​μ2=α^224​π​∑iNic​γi​Qi2.\mu^{2}{d\hat{\alpha}\over d\mu^{2}}={\hat{\alpha}^{2}\over 24\pi}\sum\limits_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}Q_{i}^{2}. (9)

This implies the RGE,

μ2​d​v^fd​μ2=α^24​π​Qf​∑iNic​γi​v^i​Qi,\mu^{2}{d\hat{v}_{f}\over d\mu^{2}}={\hat{\alpha}\over 24\pi}Q_{f}\sum\limits_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}\hat{v}_{i}Q_{i}, (10)

or in terms of the variable X^=∑iNic​γi​v^i​Qi\hat{X}=\sum_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}\hat{v}_{i}Q_{i},

d​X^X^=α^24​π​d​μ2μ2​∑iNic​γi​Qi2=d​α^α^,{d\hat{X}\over\hat{X}}={\hat{\alpha}\over 24\pi}{d\mu^{2}\over\mu^{2}}\sum\limits_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}Q_{i}^{2}={d\hat{\alpha}\over\hat{\alpha}}, (11)

where in the second equality we used Eq. (9). This is solved by,

sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)=α^​(μ)α^​(μ0)​sin2⁡θ^W​(μ0)+∑iNic​γi​Qi​Ti∑iNic​γi​Qi2​[1−α^​(μ)α^​(μ0)],\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu)={\hat{\alpha}(\mu)\over\hat{\alpha}(\mu_{0})}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu_{0})+{\sum_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}Q_{i}T_{i}\over\sum_{i}N^{c}_{i}\gamma_{i}Q_{i}^{2}}\left[1-{\hat{\alpha}(\mu)\over\hat{\alpha}(\mu_{0})}\right], (12)

or using the explicit solution to the one-loop RGE in Eq. (9) we obtain the simpler form,

sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)=sin2⁡θ^W​(μ0)​[1+α^​(μ)24​π​sin2⁡θ^W​(μ0)​∑iNic​γi​Qi​[Ti−Qi​sin2⁡θ^W​(μ0)]​ln⁡μ02μ2].\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu)=\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu_{0})\left[1+{\hat{\alpha}(\mu)\over 24\pi\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu_{0})}\sum\limits_{i}N_{i}^{c}\gamma_{i}Q_{i}[T_{i}-Q_{i}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu_{0})]\ln{\mu_{0}^{2}\over\mu^{2}}\right]. (13)

The result in Eq. (13) re-sums all logarithms of 𝒪⁡(αn​lnn​μ0μ){\cal O}(\alpha^{n}\ln^{n}{\mu_{0}\over\mu}) provided there is no particle threshold between μ\mu and μ0\mu_{0}. To avoid reintroduction of spurious logarithms this solution must be applied successively from one particle threshold to the next. Crossing a threshold from above, the corresponding particle is integrated out, and one continues with an effective field theory without this particle. In contrast, changing from one effective field theory to another far away from the physical mass of the particle would not formally affect the truncated one-loop result, but it would spoil its re-summation.

Eq. (13) applied to Δ​κ​(0)\Delta\kappa(0) can be brought into the well-known form [14],

Δ​κ​(0)=απ​s^Z2​[16​∑fNfc​Qf​(Tf−2​Qf​s^Z2)​ln⁡MZ2mf2−(4324−74​s^Z2)​ln⁡MZ2MW2],\Delta\kappa(0)={\alpha\over\pi\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}}\left[{1\over 6}\sum\limits_{f}N_{f}^{c}Q_{f}(T_{f}-2Q_{f}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z})\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over m_{f}^{2}}-\left({43\over 24}-{7\over 4}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}\right)\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over M_{W}^{2}}\right], (14)

where the sum is over all SM Dirac fermions excluding the top quark. The last term is the W±W^{\pm} contribution with its coefficient obtainable from Table 1 when a pair of massless gauge bosons (Ti=±1T_{i}=\pm 1) is combined with a complex scalar Goldstone degree of freedom (Ti=±1/2T_{i}=\pm 1/2).

4 Matching conditions

At the threshold of fermion ff we find,

sin2⁡θ^W​(mi)−=α^​(mi)−α^​(mi)+​sin2⁡θ^W​(mi)++Qi​Ti2​Qi2​[1−α^​(mi)−α^​(mi)+],\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(m_{i})^{-}={\hat{\alpha}(m_{i})^{-}\over\hat{\alpha}(m_{i})^{+}}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(m_{i})^{+}+{Q_{i}T_{i}\over 2Q_{i}^{2}}\left[1-{\hat{\alpha}(m_{i})^{-}\over\hat{\alpha}(m_{i})^{+}}\right], (26)

where the plus (minus) superscript denote the effective theory including (excluding) fermion ff. While the one and two-loop β\beta-function coefficients are well-known to be renormalization scheme independent, the matching conditions are renormalization scheme and even regularization scheme dependent. The MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme is defined by dimensional regularization which generates no 𝒪⁡(α){\cal O}(\alpha) matching terms for scalars; with the usual additional requirement66 6 Other definitions do occur in the literature, however. that the Clifford algebra is kept in four dimensions the same holds for spin-1/2 fermions. 5 Hadronic contribution

The ambiguity in the values of the three light quark masses plus the singlet contribution to Eq. (25) introduce four sources of hadronic uncertainties in sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0). This problem is familiar from the evaluation of α⁡(MZ)\alpha(M_{Z}), where it can be addressed by relating it via a dispersion relation to e+​e−→e^{+}e^{-}\to hadrons cross section data, or (using in addition isospin symmetry) to τ\tau decay spectral functions. The same strategy could in principle be applied here, except that the experimental information would have to be separated in charge 2/3 (uu) vs. charge −1/3-1/3 (dd and ss) quarks, or assuming isospin symmetry, in ss vs. the first generation quarks. This is a difficult task: e.g., a K±K^{\pm} final state in e+​e−e^{+}e^{-} annihilation can be produced directly through an s¯​γμ​s\bar{s}\gamma_{\mu}s current or by splitting of a gluon radiated off a quark originating from a u¯​γμ​u+d¯​γμ​d\bar{u}\gamma_{\mu}u+\bar{d}\gamma_{\mu}d (isoscalar) current. It would be even more difficult to isolate the singlet contribution. As for τ−\tau^{-} decays, the relatively large msm_{s} induces a sizable axial-vector contribution to final states with strangeness, S=−1S=-1. At least presently, it cannot be cleanly separated from the vector contribution which is the relevant one for the problem at hand. We will therefore follow a different strategy and show that the four uncertainties can be traded for the uncertainties associated with (i) the value of α^​(MZ){\hat{\alpha}}(M_{Z}), which we denote δα​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{\alpha}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), with (ii) the separation of strange and first generation quark effects, indicated by δs​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{s}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), with (iii) deviations from isospin symmetry, δCVC​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{\rm CVC}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), and with (iv) Zweig (OZI) rule deviations, δOZI​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{\rm OZI}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0).

As discussed in Section 3, the contributions of leptons and heavy quarks can be computed unambiguously in perturbation theory. Indeed, using QCD MS¯\overline{\rm MS} masses77footnotemark: 7 , m^q​(m^q)\hat{m}_{q}(\hat{m}_{q}), will provide a small truncation error, δPQCD​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{\rm PQCD}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), in the perturbative expansion (cf. the small matching coefficients in Eq. (27)). Moreover, the numerical values of m^q​(m^q)\hat{m}_{q}(\hat{m}_{q}) can be determined to sufficient precision that is not limited by uncertainties of the order of hadronic scales. Therefore, we compute first sin2⁡θ^W​(μ¯)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\bar{\mu}) from sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) (which can be taken from ZZ pole experiments), where μ¯\bar{\mu} corresponds to a scale where the heavy flavors (bb, cc, and τ\tau) are integrated out, and at which we still have sufficient confidence in the convergence of perturbative QCD (i.e., of order 1 GeV).

We constrain the contributions of light quarks to sin2⁡θ^W​(μ¯)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\bar{\mu}) phenomenologically. Our strategy is to employ the uu, dd, and ss quark contributions to α^​(μ¯)\hat{\alpha}(\bar{\mu}), Δ​α^(3)​(μ¯)\Delta\hat{\alpha}^{(3)}(\bar{\mu}), as a constraint, and to find upper and lower bounds on the strange quark contribution relative to the contributions of the first generation quarks. In the following we assume isospin symmetry and a vanishing singlet contribution. Deviations from these assumptions will be addressed in Section 6.

To facilitate the discussion, we will adopt definitions of threshold quark masses, m¯u\bar{m}_{u}, m¯d\bar{m}_{d}, and m¯s\bar{m}_{s}, such that Eq. (25) remains valid with trivial matching conditions, αi+​(m¯q)=αi−​(m¯q)\alpha_{i}^{+}(\bar{m}_{q})=\alpha_{i}^{-}(\bar{m}_{q}). Thus, m¯u\bar{m}_{u}, m¯d\bar{m}_{d}, and m¯s\bar{m}_{s} define the ranges in Table 2. Their values can be constrained phenomenologically99 9 See Ref. [25] for an earlier determination., but their relation to other mass definitions, such as constituent masses or current masses, cannot be written down in a perturbative sense. One combination of the three light quark threshold masses is constrained to reproduce α^​(μ¯)/α\hat{\alpha}(\bar{\mu})/\alpha. If we assume isospin symmetry, m¯u=m¯d\bar{m}_{u}=\bar{m}_{d}, and a vanishing singlet contribution, we have only one unknown parameter, say m¯s\bar{m}_{s}, to describe δs​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{s}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0). Before we use physics arguments to constrain m¯s\bar{m}_{s}, we compute m¯c\bar{m}_{c} and m¯b\bar{m}_{b} perturbatively to gauge the behavior of heavy quarks. To order αs2\alpha_{s}^{2} we have [20, 21],

which implies,

The heavy m¯s\bar{m}_{s} limit

To obtain a lower limit on the strange quark contribution to α^​(μ¯)\hat{\alpha}(\bar{\mu}), we consider the case in which the strange quark is assumed to behave like a heavy quark. In this case, m¯s\bar{m}_{s} would be related to MϕM_{\phi} in a similar way as m¯c\bar{m}_{c} (or m^c​(m^c)\hat{m}_{c}(\hat{m}_{c})) is related1010 10 More precisely, QCD sum rules relate m¯c\bar{m}_{c} (m¯b\bar{m}_{b}) rigorously to a weighted sum over Ψ\Psi (Υ\Upsilon) resonances plus a continuum contribution. For the present consideration we restrict ourselves to the lowest lying resonance which carries the largest weight. to MJ/ΨM_{J/\Psi}. 6 Uncertainties

From Eq. (39), as well as the sum of Eqs. (43) and (44), we can bound the uncertainty induced by Δ​α(3)​(m¯c)\Delta\alpha^{(3)}(\bar{m}_{c}),

δαsin2θ^W(0)<δΔα(3)(m¯c)[12−s^2(m¯c)]=±3×10−5.\delta_{\alpha}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)<\delta\Delta\alpha^{(3)}(\bar{m}_{c})\left[{1\over 2}-\hat{s}^{2}(\bar{m}_{c})\right]=\pm 3\times 10^{-5}. (45)

Similarly, from the first Eq. (42) and from the comparison of the coefficients in Eqs. (43) and (44), we can estimate the uncertainty induced by Δ​α(2)​(m¯s)\Delta\alpha^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s}),

δssin2θ^W(0)≈120δΔα(2)(m¯s)=±5×10−5.\delta_{s}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)\approx{1\over 20}\delta\Delta\alpha^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s})=\pm 5\times 10^{-5}. (46)

The singlet contribution

We obtained the theoretical bounds on m¯s\bar{m}_{s} that are the basis for the error estimate (46) by assuming isopsin symmetry and a vanishing singlet contribution. We now relax the latter assumption and allow OZI rule [?–?] violation which leads to processes such as ϕ→π0​γ\phi\to\pi^{0}\gamma decays and which translates on a diagrammatic level to QCD annihilation (singlet) topologies. For charm and third generation quarks singlet contributions are tiny and easily included using Eq. (17) or Eq. (24). We can then proceed with the effective theory containing only the three light quarks. Notice, that due to Qu+Qd+Qs=0Q_{u}+Q_{d}+Q_{s}=0, there is no singlet contribution (to the β\beta-functions of neither α\alpha nor sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W}) in the limit of exact S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry (see also the sixth entry for λ4\lambda_{4} in Table 2). Moreover, allowing S​U​(3)SU(3) breaking effects — but still working in the isospin symmetric limit — will not directly affect the RGE (20) because Tu+Td=0T_{u}+T_{d}=0. The explicit singlet piece in Eq. (25) is an artifact of employing Eq. (19) and cancels the implicit singlet piece contained in the term proportional to λ1\lambda_{1}. Not being able to isolate the implicit piece phenomenologically or to calculate the explicit piece in the non-perturbative domain introduces an additional uncertainty, which we now argue is rather small.

Perturbation theory provides an order of magnitude estimate if one assumes that the leading order perturbative coefficient is of typical size and not accidentally small. Then one would find for the singlet contribution,

δOZI​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)∼λ4​α^π​[3​α^sπ]2​5324​11−24​ζ​(3)33−2​nq∼10−6,\delta_{\rm OZI}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)\sim\lambda_{4}{\hat{\alpha}\over\pi}\left[3{\hat{\alpha}_{s}\over\pi}\right]^{2}{5\over 324}{11-24\zeta(3)\over 33-2n_{q}}\sim 10^{-6}, (47)

where the QCD expansion parameter in square brackets has been assumed to have grown in the non-perturbative regime to a number of 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1), and where nq=2n_{q}=2 and λ4=1/20\lambda_{4}=1/20 correspond to the effective field theory with the strange quark integrated out. More generally, based on results of Ref. [34] we anticipate that in leading order in NCN_{C} the singlet terms are of the form,

δOZI​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)∼λ4​α^π​[CA​α^sπ]n​TF​CF​NCCA2​Cn∼190​α^π=2.6×10−5,\delta_{\rm OZI}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)\sim\lambda_{4}{\hat{\alpha}\over\pi}\left[C_{A}{\hat{\alpha}_{s}\over\pi}\right]^{n}{T_{F}C_{F}N_{C}\over C_{A}^{2}}C_{n}\sim{1\over 90}{\hat{\alpha}\over\pi}=2.6\times 10^{-5}, (48)

where the QCD group factors are TF=1/2T_{F}=1/2, CF=4/3C_{F}=4/3, CA=NC=3C_{A}=N_{C}=3, and where the coefficients CnC_{n} are expected to be of 𝒪⁡(1){\cal O}(1). An alternative form can be written down relative to Δ​α(2)​(m¯s)\Delta\alpha^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s}) in Eq. (42),

δOZI​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)∼λ4​Δ​α(2)​(m¯s)Qu2+Qd2​TFCA=3200​Δ​α(2)​(m¯s)=(2.6∓1.4)×10−5,\delta_{\rm OZI}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)\sim\lambda_{4}{\Delta\alpha^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s})\over{Q_{u}^{2}+Q_{d}^{2}}}{T_{F}\over C_{A}}={3\over 200}\Delta\alpha^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s})=(2.6\mp 1.4)\times 10^{-5}, (49)

which incidentally gives the same result. These forms exhibits all QED charges and leading QCD group factors explicitly, which combined lead to a suppression of the singlet contribution by two orders of magnitude relative to the non-singlet contribution. Thus, the smallness of the estimate in Eq. (47) is in part due to C2≈−0.043≪1C_{2}\approx-0.043\ll 1 (which may or may not reflect the typical size of the other CnC_{n}), and in part due to the suppression factors displayed in Eqs. (48) and (49) which will apply at any order. In particular, OZI rule violating effects are absent in leading order in the 1/NC1/N_{C} expansion.

In Appendix B we will test these order of magnitude estimates by studying the masses and mixings of vector mesons (which strongly dominate the real parts of the vector current correlators). The results obtained there turn out to be in line with the estimate (47), but conservatively we base our final uncertainty on Eqs. (48) and (49) and take,

δOZIsin2θ^W(0)=±3×10−5.\delta_{\rm OZI}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=\pm 3\times 10^{-5}. (50)

Isospin breaking

So far we have assumed exact isopsin symmetry. Recall that the S​U​(3)SU(3) limit serves to maximize the RGE running of sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W} by minimizing the effective down-type quark masses relative to m¯u\bar{m}_{u}. Allowing m¯d>m¯u\bar{m}_{d}>\bar{m}_{u} can therefore only strengthen this limit. Thus, the uncertainty associated with isospin symmetry breaking, δCVC​sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\delta_{\rm CVC}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0), is asymmetric.

As for the heavy m¯s\bar{m}_{s} limit, we proceed by considering the hypothetical reference case, m¯d=m¯s≠m¯u\bar{m}_{d}=\bar{m}_{s}\neq\bar{m}_{u}. In our framework this corresponds to maximal S​U​(2)SU(2) (CVC) violation, i.e., S​U​(2)SU(2) breaking is of the same size as S​U​(3)SU(3) breaking. The inequality, Δ​α^(2)​(m¯s)<0.00262\Delta\hat{\alpha}^{(2)}(\bar{m}_{s})<0.00262 (see Eq. (42)), would be replaced by,

Δ​α^(1)​(m¯d)<0.00262,\Delta\hat{\alpha}^{(1)}(\bar{m}_{d})<0.00262, (51)

which bounds the up quark contribution for energy scales below the down-type quark effective masses. λ1=3/8\lambda_{1}=3/8 now to be used in Eq. (25) in place of λ1=9/20\lambda_{1}=9/20 in the isospin symmetric case would cause a shift,

δCVCsin2θ^W(0)=−340Δα^(1)(m¯d)>−2×10−4.\delta_{\rm CVC}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=-{3\over 40}\Delta\hat{\alpha}^{(1)}(\bar{m}_{d})>-2\times 10^{-4}. (52)

A measure of S​U​(2)SU(2) breaking relative to S​U​(3)SU(3) breaking is given by the ratio,

|M¯K∗⁣±2−M¯K∗02M¯K∗⁣±2−M¯ρ02|≈0.04,\left|{\bar{M}_{K^{*\pm}}^{2}-\bar{M}_{K^{*0}}^{2}\over\bar{M}_{K^{*\pm}}^{2}-\bar{M}_{\rho^{0}}^{2}}\right|\approx 0.04, (53)

which leads to the estimate,

δCVCsin2θ^W(0)=−8+0×10−6,\delta_{\rm CVC}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=^{+0}_{-8}\times 10^{-6}, (54)

and shows that isospin breaking affects our analysis at a very small level.

Other uncertainties

In the perturbative regime we used theory in place of experimental data, which induces two kinds of uncertainties: purely theoretical ones and parametric ones from the input quark masses and αs\alpha_{s}. The former include the errors associated with the truncation of perturbation theory and with non-perturbative effects. We estimate their size to about ±7×10−5\pm 7\times 10^{-5}. However, this uncertainty is already included in Eq. (39) where it propagates properly correlated to the error of the low energy weak mixing angle. The uncertainties in the quark masses induce an error of ±4×10−5\pm 4\times 10^{-5} which is dominated by m^c​(m^c)\hat{m}_{c}(\hat{m}_{c}). The uncertainty in αs\alpha_{s} induces an error of the same size. In practice, these parametric uncertainties and the one from Eq. (39) are included in global fits to all data where these parameters are allowed to float subject to experimental and theoretical constraints, and where correlations are naturally accounted for. The same applies to the experimental uncertainties in sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) and MZM_{Z}. These have almost no effect on κ^​(0)\hat{\kappa}(0), but if the absolute normalization of s^2​(0)\hat{s}^{2}(0) is required they induce errors of ±1.4×10−4\pm 1.4\times 10^{-4} and ±1.4×10−5\pm 1.4\times 10^{-5}, respectively.

The theoretical uncertainties (45), (46), (50), and (54) added in quadrature yield a total theory error,

δtheorysin2θ^W(0)=±7×10−5.\delta_{\rm theory}\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=\pm 7\times 10^{-5}. (55)

This is almost an order of magnitude more precise than the result obtained some time ago in Ref. [15]. Using our results in a global fit to precision data yields,

sin2⁡θ^W​(0)=0.23867±0.00016.\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0)=0.23867\pm 0.00016. (56)

The central value coincides with Ref. [36] where a seemingly independent definition of the low energy mixing angle (based on gauge invariance and the pinch-technique) is introduced. We will comment more on the relation between our work and Ref. [36] in the following Section. The uncertainty in Eq. (56) is completely dominated by the experimental uncertainty,

δsin2θ^W(MZ)=±1.5×10−4.\delta\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z})=\pm 1.5\times 10^{-4}. (57)

7 Other considerations

Some time ago, the authors of Refs. [10, 11] suggested that the use of an appropriate, scale-dependent effective weak mixing angle could provide a useful means of comparing the results of various neutral current experiments at the Z0Z^{0}-pole and below. By now, it is conventional to compare the value of an effective weak mixing angle extracted from experimental results with its predicted value in the Standard Model (see, e.g., Ref. [8]). More recently, it was observed [36] that the effective weak mixing angle derived from the sum of ZZ-γ\gamma mixing diagrams evaluated in the RξR_{\xi} gauge and frequently used to interpret low energy neutral current experiments is not gauge invariant. This sin2⁡θ^​(q2)eff\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff} is defined analogously to Eq. (5) with a scheme- and q2q^{2}-dependent form factor, κ^​(q2)\hat{\kappa}(q^{2}),

sin2⁡θ^​(q2)eff≡Re⁡[κ^​(q2,μ=MZ)]​sin2⁡θ^W​(μ=MZ).\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff}\equiv{\rm Re}[\hat{\kappa}(q^{2},\mu=M_{Z})]\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu=M_{Z}). (58)

In the MS¯{\overline{\rm MS}}-scheme, both κ^\hat{\kappa} and sin2⁡θ^W\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W} depend on the renormalization scale μ\mu, while κ^\hat{\kappa} also carries a q2q^{2}-dependence. The authors of Ref. [36] note that the κ^​(q2,μ)\hat{\kappa}(q^{2},\mu) form factor naively-defined in terms of ZZ-γ\gamma mixing depends on the choice of electroweak gauge so that the corresponding sin2⁡θ​(q2)eff\sin^{2}\theta(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff} is not a physically meaningful quantity. By itself, this gauge dependence is not particularly problematic, since for any physical observable — such as the parity violating Møller asymmetry computed in Ref. [10] — it is canceled by the gauge dependence of other radiative corrections, leaving a gauge independent result. Nevertheless, if one wishes to isolate a particular class of radiative corrections, such as those entering sin2⁡θ^​(q2)eff\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff}, one usually prefers to discuss gauge invariant quantities, especially when the comparison of different experimental results is involved.

The authors of Ref. [36] show that one may, indeed, obtain a gauge independent κ^​(q2,μ)\hat{\kappa}(q^{2},\mu) by including the so-called “pinch parts” of various one-loop vertex and box diagrams that are process independent and that compensate for the gauge dependence of the naive κ^\hat{\kappa} form factor. Here, we comment on the relationship between sin2⁡θ^​(q2)eff\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff} of Ref. [36] and sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) discussed in our work and observe that they are identical at one-loop order.

For |q2|<MW2|q^{2}|<M_{W}^{2}, the gauge invariant form factor κ^\hat{\kappa} of Ref. [36] is given by,

κ^​(q2,μ)PT\displaystyle{\hat{\kappa}}(q^{2},\mu)^{\rm PT} =\displaystyle= 1+α2​π​s^Z2lnMZ2μ2[−13∑fNfcQf(Tf−2Qfs^Z2)+72c^Z2+112]\displaystyle 1+{\alpha\over 2\pi\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}}\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over\mu^{2}}\left[-{1\over 3}\sum\limits_{f}N_{f}^{c}Q_{f}(T_{f}-2Q_{f}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z})+{7\over 2}{\hat{c}}^{2}_{Z}+{1\over 12}\right] (59)
−α2​π​s^Z2​[2​∑fNfc​Qf​(Tf−2​Qf​s^Z2)​If​(q2)+(72​c^Z2+112)​ln⁡MZ2MW2+c^Z23],\displaystyle-{\alpha\over 2\pi\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}}\left[2\sum\limits_{f}N_{f}^{c}Q_{f}(T_{f}-2Q_{f}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z})I_{f}(q^{2})+\left({7\over 2}{\hat{c}}^{2}_{Z}+{1\over 12}\right)\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over M_{W}^{2}}+{{\hat{c}}^{2}_{Z}\over 3}\right],

where,

If​(q2)=∫01d​x​x​(1−x)​ln⁡mf2−q2​x​(1−x)MZ2,I_{f}(q^{2})=\int_{0}^{1}\ dxx(1-x)\ln{m_{f}^{2}-q^{2}x(1-x)\over M_{Z}^{2}}, (60)

and where the PT superscript in Eq. (59) indicates the gauge invariant “pinch-technique” definition of the form factor. For μ=MZ\mu=M_{Z}, the second term on the right hand side of Eq. (59) vanishes. The integrals If​(q2)I_{f}(q^{2}) in the third term generate the large logarithms containing fermion masses that one would like to re-sum. As discussed in Section 1, this re-summation is accomplished by choosing μ∼|q2|\mu\sim\sqrt{|q^{2}|} rather than μ=MZ\mu=M_{Z}, thereby eliminating these logarithms from κ^​(q2,μ)PT{\hat{\kappa}}(q^{2},\mu)^{\rm PT} altogether and moving them instead into sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(\mu), which we analyze in this paper. The RGE for sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(\mu) then provides for the desired re-summation. Similarly, the term proportional to ln⁡MZ2/MW2\ln M_{Z}^{2}/M_{W}^{2} in Eq. (59) corresponds to the weak gauge sector contributions to the RGE running from μ=MZ\mu=M_{Z} down to MWM_{W}. Below this scale, the heavy gauge bosons are to be integrated out.

It is not too surprising that the logarithms appearing, for example, in Eq. (14), are identical to those obtained from the PT since it has been shown [37] that the asymptotic behavior of effective coupling constants directly constructed from the PT self-energies are automatically governed by the renormalization group. Now we observe that even the non-logarithmic piece in the third term of Eq. (59) can be understood in the context of the renormalization group, except that in this case it arises from RGE matching rather than RGE running. In Ref. [36] the c^Z2/3{\hat{c}}^{2}_{Z}/3 term results from combining the pinch parts of the one-loop vertex and box graphs with the remaining weak gauge-dependent contributions to the γ​Z\gamma Z-mixing tensor. The precise value for this μ\mu-independent constant follows from the requirement that κ^​(q2,μ)PT{\hat{\kappa}}(q^{2},\mu)^{\rm PT} be gauge invariant. In our treatment of the running sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(\mu), this same constant is generated by the threshold corrections at μ=MW\mu=M_{W} given in Eqs. (29) and (30). Indeed, use of the RGE with appropriate matching conditions may provide a more direct route for obtaining the results of Ref. [36] while allowing one to generalize it to include various higher-order effects as we have done.

It follows as a corollary that the PT applied within the DR¯\overline{\rm DR}-scheme (compare the last footnote in Section 4) should not yield any constant terms at one-loop order. As a particular application, one may consider the correspondence between the two treatments at μ=0\mu=0. Eqs. (12), (29), and (30) show that the relation between sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(0) and sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(M_{Z})

sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\displaystyle\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(0) =\displaystyle= sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\displaystyle\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(M_{Z}) (61)
+\displaystyle+ απ​[16​∑fNfc​Qf​(Tf−2​Qf​s^Z2)​ln⁡MZ2mf2−(4324−74​s^Z2)​ln⁡MZ2MW2−16​c^Z2],\displaystyle{\alpha\over\pi}\left[{1\over 6}\sum\limits_{f}N_{f}^{c}Q_{f}(T_{f}-2Q_{f}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z})\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over m_{f}^{2}}-\left({43\over 24}-{7\over 4}\hat{s}^{2}_{Z}\right)\ln{M_{Z}^{2}\over M_{W}^{2}}-{1\over 6}\hat{c}^{2}_{Z}\right],

is the electroweak analog of the relation between the electromagnetic fine structure constant, α=α^​(0)\alpha=\hat{\alpha}(0) and α^​(MZ)\hat{\alpha}(M_{Z}). Note that a similar relation would hold for other definitions of the weak mixing angle and the corresponding definition of the running QED coupling in the same scheme. For example, different conventions for the treatment of heavy top quark effects [5] would affect the definitions of sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(M_{Z}) and α^​(MZ)\hat{\alpha}(M_{Z}), but the right-hand side of relation (61) would also have to be modified with the net effect that the left-hand side would remain unchanged. Nonetheless, we reiterate that the definition (61) is gauge invariant because it agrees with sin2⁡θ^​(q2=0)eff\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2}=0)^{\rm\;eff}, and that the analysis of Section 3 has allowed us to incorporate higher order effects in α\alpha and αs\alpha_{s} into sin2⁡θW\sin^{2}\theta_{W}. Note also that if sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(\mu) or sin2⁡θ^​(q2)eff\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}(q^{2})^{\rm\;eff} are used in low |q2||q^{2}| amplitudes, care must be taken to consistently include other radiative corrections in the same scheme.

While our study has focused on sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}{\hat{\theta}}_{W}(\mu) appropriate for low |q2||q^{2}| processes, it is also worth commenting on the running of the weak mixing angle above the weak scale. For |q2|≫MZ2|q^{2}|\gg M_{Z}^{2}, it is most appropriate to work in a basis involving the “primordial” S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} and U​(1)YU(1)_{Y} gauge bosons and the β\beta-functions for gg and g′g^{\prime}. Starting from Eq. (1) one obtains the RGE,

s^2​d​α^d​t−α^​d​s^2d​t=b2π​α^2+∑jb2​jπ2​α^2​α^j+⋯,{\hat{s}}^{2}{d{\hat{\alpha}}\over dt}-{\hat{\alpha}}{d{\hat{s}}^{2}\over dt}={b_{2}\over\pi}{\hat{\alpha}}^{2}+\sum_{j}{b_{2j}\over\pi^{2}}{\hat{\alpha}}^{2}{\hat{\alpha}}_{j}+\cdots, (62)

where t=ln⁡μt=\ln\mu, and where b2b_{2} and b2​jb_{2j} are, respectively, the one- and two-loop β\beta-function coefficients involving S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} (see,e.g., Ref. [38]). The solution to Eq. (62) can be written in the same form as Eq. (25). We note, however, that a naive application of the RGE (62) to scales μ≪MW\mu\ll M_{W} would not re-sum all the large logarithms associated with the low |q2||q^{2}| radiative corrections. For example, from Eq. (62) one obtains,

λ1=∑qTq22​∑qQq2.\lambda_{1}={\sum_{q}T_{q}^{2}\over 2\sum_{q}Q_{q}^{2}}. (63)

So long as both members of a quark doublet are included in the effective theory, this result is equivalent to the expression in Eq. (21), since Q=T+YQ=T+Y and Tr⁡(T​Y)=0{\rm Tr\,}(TY)=0, where YY denotes hypercharge. However, for μ\mu lying between the masses of two doublet members, this equivalence no longer holds, and only Eq. (21) will lead to a full re-summation of the large logarithms.

8 Conclusions and outlook

With the completion of the precision electroweak programs at LEP 1, SLC, and LEP 2, precision measurements of low energy neutral current observables have taken on added interest in recent years. A useful way to compare the results from existing and prospective experiments is to extract the value of the weak mixing angle that each would imply, assuming no other physics than that of the SM. The extent of their agreement with the SM prediction for this quantity provides important information about both the SM as well as the various scenarios that might extend it.

The impact of this low energy precision program depends on both the precision of the various experiments as well as that of the SM predictions. In this study, we have attempted to refine the latter by giving the appropriate low energy running weak mixing angle in the MS¯{\overline{\rm MS}}-scheme, sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu). By using this quantity and taking μ2∼|q2|\mu^{2}\sim|q^{2}|, one is able to re-sum various logarithmically-enhanced contributions that would otherwise appear in the radiative corrections for |q2|≪MW2|q^{2}|\ll M_{W}^{2}, thereby reducing the truncation error associated with the perturbative expansion. At one-loop order, this re-summation reproduces the result of Ref. [36], but we have been able to generalize that work to include higher order contributions in α\alpha and αs\alpha_{s}. We have also provided an extensive analysis of the non-perturbative hadronic contributions to sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) for μ∼0\mu\sim 0 and argued that the associated uncertainties enter below the 10−410^{-4} level.

The resulting scale-dependence of sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) for μ=|q2|\mu=\sqrt{|q^{2}|} with q2q^{2} being the four-momentum transfer squared is shown in Fig. 1. The various discontinuities in the curve correspond to the thresholds discussed above, while the size of the theoretical uncertainty in the curve corresponds to its thickness.

As a particular application, we obtained a definition of the mixing angle in the Thomson limit, sin2⁡θW≡sin2⁡θ^W​(0)\sin^{2}\theta_{W}\equiv\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(0) whose relation with the value determined at the ZZ-pole sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) is the electroweak analog of the relation between the fine structure α=α^​(0)\alpha=\hat{\alpha}(0) constant and α^​(MZ)\hat{\alpha}(M_{Z}). This definition also coincides with the gauge invariant definition recently constructed in Ref. [36], and its numerical value is

sin2⁡θW=0.23867±0.00016,\sin^{2}\theta_{W}=0.23867\pm 0.00016, (64)

where the error is dominated by the experimental error from ZZ pole measurements. From its relation to the MS¯\overline{\rm MS}-scheme mixing angle at the ZZ scale, sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}), by Eq. (7), we obtain

Δ​κ^​(0)=0.03232±0.00029,\Delta\hat{\kappa}(0)=0.03232\pm 0.00029, (65)

where now the error is purely theoretical. Finally, using the relation [48] between sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) and the effective leptonic mixing angle, sin2⁡θfeff\sin^{2}\theta_{f}^{\rm\;eff}, defined in Eq. (5), we obtain,

sin2⁡θW−sin2⁡θℓeff=0.00718±0.00007.\sin^{2}\theta_{W}-\sin^{2}\theta_{\ell}^{\rm\;eff}=0.00718\pm 0.00007. (66)

The error in this relation (which is the main result of this work) is an order of magnitude below current and anticipated experimental uncertainties and considerably smaller than the uncertainty quoted in Refs. [15].

To illustrate the impact of this result on particular observables, we consider the weak charge of the proton, QW​(p)Q_{W}(p), that will be determined using parity-violating elastic e​pep scattering at the Jefferson Lab. Up-dating the recent analysis of Ref. [39], we obtain the Standard Model prediction

QW​(p)\displaystyle Q_{W}(p) =\displaystyle= 0.0713±0.0006​(input)±0.0003​(Δ​κ^)±0.0005​(Z​γ​box)±0.0001​(W​W​box)\displaystyle 0.0713\pm 0.0006~({\rm input})\pm 0.0003~(\Delta\hat{\kappa})\pm 0.0005~(Z\gamma\ {\rm box})\pm 0.0001~(WW\ {\rm box}) (67)
=\displaystyle= 0.0713±0.0008,\displaystyle 0.0713\pm 0.0008,

where the experimental uncertainties in sin2⁡θ^W​(MZ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(M_{Z}) and mtm_{t} (“input”), the theoretical hadronic uncertainties in Δ​κ^​(0)\Delta\hat{\kappa}(0) and the Z​γZ\gamma box graph, and the uncertainty from unknown higher-order perturbative QCD contributions to the W​WWW box graphs are shown separately and combined in quadrature in the second line. Use of the previous estimate for the uncertainty in Δ​κ^​(0)\Delta\hat{\kappa}(0) of ±0.0025\pm 0.0025 would lead to a theoretical (total) error in the QW​(p)Q_{W}(p) prediction roughly five (three) times larger than in Eq. (67), and in this case, one could neglect the uncertainties associated with other radiative corrections. In light of our analysis, however, the uncertainty in the Standard Model prediction is now three and a half times smaller than the anticipated experimental error, and theoretical uncertainties associated with hadronic contributions to other radiative corrections become relatively more important.

In the same vein, the interpretation of the prospective parity violating deep inelastic measurements will require a careful analysis of higher twist and isospin breaking corrections, especially given that the latter may be responsible for the present discrepancy between the NuTeV result for sin2⁡θ^W​(μ∼3​GeV)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu\sim 3\ {\rm GeV}) and the SM prediction. Our analysis applies to the deep inelastic regime, as well, where due to the higher energies involved, the uncertainty in sin2⁡θ^W​(μ)\sin^{2}\hat{\theta}_{W}(\mu) is even much smaller since no complications from non-perturbative contributions arise in this case. Given the level of experimental effort required to carry out these precise low energy measurements, performing a theoretical analysis of these effects at the level we have attempted to do here for the weak mixing angle seems well-worth the effort.

Appendix A Updated value for the mixing angle ϵ\epsilon

Here we determine the phenomenological value of the ω\omega-ϕ\phi mixing angle, ϵ\epsilon, defined by,

|ω⟩=cos⁡ϵ​|u¯​u⟩+|d¯​d⟩2−sin⁡ϵ⁡|s¯​s⟩,|ϕ⟩=sin⁡ϵ​|u¯​u⟩+|d¯​d⟩2+cos⁡ϵ⁡|s¯​s⟩,|\omega\rangle=\cos\epsilon{|\bar{u}u\rangle+|\bar{d}d\rangle\over\sqrt{2}}-\sin\epsilon|\bar{s}s\rangle,\hskip 50.0pt|\phi\rangle=\sin\epsilon{|\bar{u}u\rangle+|\bar{d}d\rangle\over\sqrt{2}}+\cos\epsilon|\bar{s}s\rangle, (68)

where ϵ=0\epsilon=0 is referred to as ideal mixing. One way to extract it is to use S​U​(3)SU(3) flavor symmetry and first order breaking applied to the vector meson octet mass spectrum. An advantage of this method is that it can be calibrated against the ground state baryon octet, for which Fermi statistics precludes the mixing with an S​U​(3)SU(3) singlet state. The mass of the S​U​(2)SU(2) singlet, MΛM_{\Lambda}, is therefore predicted in terms of the masses of the other electrically neutral octet members,

MΛ=13​(2​Mn+2​MΞ0−MΣ0)=1105.4​ MeV,M_{\Lambda}={1\over 3}(2M_{n}+2M_{\Xi^{0}}-M_{\Sigma^{0}})=1105.4\mbox{ MeV}, (69)

which reproduces the experimental value [40], MΛ=1115.7M_{\Lambda}=1115.7 MeV, within 0.93%. Analogously, the Gell-Mann-Okubo mass formula [41, 42] yields the octet-octet component of the mass matrix for the isosinglet ground state vector mesons,

M¯882=13​(4​M¯K∗02−M¯ρ02)=(933.69​ MeV)2×[1±0.0008±0.0020±0.0121±0.0093].\bar{M}_{88}^{2}={1\over 3}(4\bar{M}^{2}_{K^{*0}}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}})=(933.69\mbox{ MeV})^{2}\times[1\pm 0.0008\pm 0.0020\pm 0.0121\pm 0.0093]. (70)

The first error is from the experimental uncertainty in the masses, which are taken from Ref. [40] except for the mass, Mρ0=775.74±0.65M_{\rho^{0}}=775.74\pm 0.65 MeV, and the width, Γρ0=145.3±1.4\Gamma_{\rho^{0}}=145.3\pm 1.4 MeV, of the ρ0\rho^{0} resonance for which we averaged Refs. [43, 44]. The broadness of some of the resonances involved introduces an ambiguity as for what definition of mass one should use in the Gell-Mann-Okubo formula. For the central value we have chosen the peak position,

M¯=M1+Γ2M24,\bar{M}={M\over\sqrt[4]{1+{\Gamma^{2}\over M^{2}}}}, (71)

where MM and Γ\Gamma correspond to the usual definition of a relativistic Breit-Wigner resonance form with an ss-dependent width, i.e. the one used by the Particle Data Group [40]. The second error in Eq. (70) reflects the size of the shift obtained by replacing M¯\bar{M} by MM. The third error is due to possible isospin breaking effects which we estimated by using M¯K∗⁣±2\bar{M}^{2}_{K^{*\pm}} in place of M¯K∗02\bar{M}^{2}_{K^{*0}}. The last error quantifies the limitation of the method and is given by the calibration against the baryon octet as discussed above. Adding all errors in quadrature, we obtain for the S​U​(3)SU(3) octet-singlet mixing angle [40], θV\theta_{V},

tan2⁡θV=M¯882−M¯ϕ2M¯ω2−M¯882=0.646+0.090−0.081,\tan^{2}\theta_{V}=\frac{\bar{M}_{88}^{2}-\bar{M}_{\phi}^{2}}{\bar{M}_{\omega}^{2}-\bar{M}_{88}^{2}}=0.646^{-0.081}_{+0.090}, (72)

which translates into the two solutions1313 13 Since Γϕ≪Mϕ\Gamma_{\phi}\ll M_{\phi} and Γω≪Mω\Gamma_{\omega}\ll M_{\omega}, the complex phase in ϵ\epsilon can safely be neglected., ϵ1=0.061∓0.032\epsilon_{1}=0.061\mp 0.032 and ϵ2=−1.292±0.032\epsilon_{2}=-1.292\pm 0.032. Alternatively, one can compare the branching ratios of the ω\omega and ϕ\phi resonances decaying into π0​γ\pi^{0}\gamma [45],

tan2⁡ϵ=Mϕ3Mω3​(Mω2−Mπ02Mϕ2−Mπ02)3​ℬ⁡(ϕ→π0​γ)ℬ⁡(ω→π0​γ)​ΓϕΓω=(3.01±0.26)×10−3,\tan^{2}\epsilon={M_{\phi}^{3}\over M_{\omega}^{3}}\left(\frac{M_{\omega}^{2}-M_{\pi^{0}}^{2}}{M_{\phi}^{2}-M_{\pi^{0}}^{2}}\right)^{3}\frac{{\cal B}(\phi\to\pi^{0}\gamma)}{{\cal B}(\omega\to\pi^{0}\gamma)}{\Gamma_{\phi}\over\Gamma_{\omega}}=(3.01\pm 0.26)\times 10^{-3}, (73)

which gives, |ϵ|=0.0548±0.0024|\epsilon|=0.0548\pm 0.0024. Comparison with the previous method singles out the solution,

ϵ=+0.0548±0.0024.\epsilon=+0.0548\pm 0.0024. (74)

The sign and magnitude are also consistent with various other methods [46] and the previous analysis in Ref. [45].

Appendix B Phenomenological approach to OZI suppression

In Section 6 we argued that the OZI rule can at least partly be understood as a result of group theoretical suppression factors relative to OZI allowed processes. Using the result of Appendix A, we now wish to study OZI rule violating contributions to the mass matrix of ground state vector mesons. These mesons dominate the electromagnetic current correlator at hadronic scales, and should therefore serve as a means to quantify OZI rule suppressions phenomenologically. Throughout this Appendix we work in the isospin symmetric limit.

In the flavor basis, (|u¯​u⟩,|d¯​d⟩,|s¯​s⟩)(|\bar{u}u\rangle,|\bar{d}d\rangle,|\bar{s}s\rangle), we write the mass matrix in a form which is similar to the one discussed in Ref. [47],

M=(A+BBB+CBA+BB+CB+CB+CA+B+D).M=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}A+B&B&B+C\\ B&A+B&B+C\\ B+C&B+C&A+B+D\end{array}\right). (75)

The parameters AA and BB respect S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry, while CC and DD break it. The off-diagonal elements, BB and CC, parametrize flavor transitions, and can only be generated by QCD annihilation (singlet) diagrams. The parameter DD receives contributions from the strange quark mass, as well as dynamical contributions of both singlet and non-singlet type. The difference to Ref. [47] is that there C=0C=0, and B=B⁡(μ)B=B(\mu) is a scale dependent singlet function, while we define all entries of MM as constants without specifying their relation to the scale dependent current correlators. In the isospin basis, (|(u¯​u−d¯​d)/2⟩,|(u¯​u+d¯​d)/2⟩,|s¯​s⟩)(|(\bar{u}u-\bar{d}d)/\sqrt{2}\rangle,|(\bar{u}u+\bar{d}d)/\sqrt{2}\rangle,|\bar{s}s\rangle), MM reads,

M=(A000A+2​B2​(B+C)02​(B+C)A+B+D),M=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}A&0&0\\ 0&A+2B&\sqrt{2}(B+C)\\ 0&\sqrt{2}(B+C)&A+B+D\end{array}\right), (76)

so that we can identify, A=M¯ρ02A=\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}}. The trace of MM then yields the condition,

3​B+D=M¯ω2+M¯ϕ2−2​M¯ρ02,3B+D=\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega}+\bar{M}^{2}_{\phi}-2\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}}, (77)

and ϵ\epsilon obtained in Appendix A gives the constraint,

tan⁡2​ϵ=8​B+CD−B.\tan 2\epsilon=\sqrt{8}{B+C\over D-B}. (78)

The final relation,

(M¯ϕ2−M¯ω2)2=[3​(B+C)−13​(C+D)]2+89​(C+D)2,(\bar{M}^{2}_{\phi}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega})^{2}=\left[3(B+C)-{1\over 3}(C+D)\right]^{2}+{8\over 9}(C+D)^{2}, (79)

shows that in the S​U​(3)SU(3) limit, C=D=0C=D=0, singlet diagrams associated with BB would split Mϕ2M^{2}_{\phi} from Mρ02=Mω2M^{2}_{\rho^{0}}=M^{2}_{\omega} in much the same way as triangle anomaly diagrams would split Mη′2M^{2}_{\eta^{\prime}} from Mη2=Mπ2M^{2}_{\eta}=M^{2}_{\pi}. Taking into account that ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1, we can approximate,

B≈M¯ω2−M¯ρ022,D≈M¯ϕ2−M¯ω2+M¯ρ022,B\approx{\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}}\over 2},\hskip 100.0ptD\approx\bar{M}^{2}_{\phi}-{\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega}+\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}}\over 2}, (80)

which is correct up to 𝒪⁡(ϵ2){\cal O}(\epsilon^{2}). Thus, in the limit of ideal mixing, BB drives the splitting of Mω2M^{2}_{\omega} from Mρ02M^{2}_{\rho^{0}} instead. In any case, the singlet contribution associated to BB is very small compared to AA and DD. More relevant for this work is the S​U​(3)SU(3) breaking singlet parameter,

C≈M¯ϕ2−M¯ω28​tan⁡2​ϵ−M¯ω2−M¯ρ022,C\approx{\bar{M}^{2}_{\phi}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega}\over\sqrt{8}}\tan 2\epsilon-{\bar{M}^{2}_{\omega}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}}\over 2}, (81)

which reduces to C=−BC=-B in the ideal mixing case, ϵ=0\epsilon=0. Numerically, we have,

A=(769​ MeV)2,B=(105​ MeV)2,C=(  74​ MeV)2,D=(660​ MeV)2.\begin{array}[]{ll}A=(769\mbox{ MeV})^{2},&B=(105\mbox{ MeV})^{2},\\ C=(\;\;74\mbox{ MeV})^{2},&D=(660\mbox{ MeV})^{2}.\end{array} (82)

There is a second solution in which |B||B|, |C||C|, and |D||D| are all comparable and where B≈−CB\approx-C to ensure ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1. It also has D<0D<0, although the strange quark mass is expected to give the dominant (positive) contribution. Therefore we discard this solution. We can also roughly estimate the singlet component contained in DD by relating it to MK∗0M_{K^{*0}},

Dsinglet∼D−2​(M¯K∗02−M¯ρ02)=(123​ MeV)2,D_{\rm singlet}\sim D-2(\bar{M}^{2}_{K^{*0}}-\bar{M}^{2}_{\rho^{0}})=(123\mbox{ MeV})^{2}, (83)

which is of similar size as BB and CC. Thus, singlet contributions to vector meson masses are generally suppressed by more than an order of magnitude beyond the QCD suppression factors discussed in Section 6 indicating that the smallness of the known coefficient, C2≪1C_{2}\ll 1, may indeed be a generic feature that persists at higher orders. Qualitatively the same results are obtained if linear mass relations are used in place of masses squared, except that singlet contributions appear even more suppressed.
